review_target: The verification design for server/migrations/004_access_control.up.sql — the 17-assertion shell/SQL check script the implementer reports running red-then-green, plus the Point B idempotency re-run. NOT the migration SQL text itself (independently verified verbatim-match to tech-spec Data Models during tech-spec/task-decomposition validation).
summary: The migration file matches spec verbatim and its operators are individually sound. The gaps are in what the described check design actually proves: several of the 17 assertions are named at the level of 'does this object exist' rather than 'does this object have the exact shape Decision 3/4/5 require', which lets classes of regression a future edit to this file could introduce slip through green. The two highest-value findings are concrete, not hypothetical: (1) three pre-existing tables (user_settings, chats, calculations) already carry a FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE — an information_schema join that isn't tightly scoped to access_requests could pass even if that table's own FK were broken or missing; (2) the task's own Acceptance Criteria demands verification against both a clean DB and a DB carrying the current prod schema (001+002+003), and migrate.go's version-skip means those are genuinely different code paths — the standard docker-compose-up smoke flow most likely only exercises the 'all four files applied together against an empty users table' path, not '004 applied standalone against a schema that already has real user rows', which is the actual production redeploy scenario.

findings.description: The design is described as covering 'schema columns... existence' — that phrasing, and the task's own TDD Anchor ('SHOW COLUMNS FROM users — содержит role, has_access, email, display_name'), reads as presence-only: does a column with this name appear in SHOW COLUMNS output. That is a materially weaker claim than what Decision 3 and Decision 4 promise: `role VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user'` and `has_access BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`. A presence check cannot distinguish the migration as written from a regression where NOT NULL or the DEFAULT clause is dropped (e.g. a future hand-edit, since down-migrations don't exist and fixes happen by hand-editing already-applied files per Decision-adjacent notes in the tech-spec). Concretely: if `role` were nullable, `CHECK (role IN ('user','admin'))` would NOT reject NULL — under standard SQL/MariaDB CHECK semantics, `NULL IN (...)` evaluates to UNKNOWN, which a CHECK constraint treats as satisfied, not violated. So a nullable role column silently defeats the 'role is always user or admin' guarantee the middleware (RequireAdmin) is described as relying on, and neither a presence-only column check nor the CHECK constraint itself would catch it. The same gap applies to `chk_access_requests_status`: the smoke text says 'SHOW CREATE TABLE access_requests — ...с ожидаемыми колонками, FK и CHECK', but doesn't say the CHECK's actual predicate (IN ('pending','approved','rejected')) is compared against the expected list rather than just 'a CHECK constraint with this name exists'.
findings.recommendation: For every column, assert the full definition line from SHOW COLUMNS (Type, Null, Default), not just Field presence — e.g. `SHOW COLUMNS FROM users WHERE Field='role'` must show `Type=varchar(16)`, `Null=NO`, `Default=user`, and likewise `has_access`: `Type=tinyint(1)` (MariaDB's BOOLEAN), `Null=NO`, `Default=0`. For both CHECK constraints, pull the actual predicate text via `SELECT CHECK_CLAUSE FROM information_schema.CHECK_CONSTRAINTS WHERE CONSTRAINT_NAME IN ('chk_users_role','chk_access_requests_status')` and assert the clause contains exactly the expected enum values, not merely that a row with that constraint name exists.

findings.description: Confirmed concretely against the actual migration files (not hypothetical): `user_settings`, `chats`, and `calculations` — all created by 0001_init.sql / 002_costing_schema.up.sql, already live in this schema before 004 ever runs — each declare `FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, the identical shape (same referencing column name, same referenced table+column, same delete rule) as `fk_access_requests_user` on `access_requests`. A join of `information_schema.key_column_usage` and `information_schema.referential_constraints` that isn't scoped tightly — e.g. joined only on `CONSTRAINT_NAME` without also requiring `TABLE_SCHEMA`/`CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA` on both sides, or checked only for 'some FK with DELETE_RULE=CASCADE pointing user_id at users(id) exists anywhere in the schema' rather than specifically on `access_requests` — can return a true/pass result sourced from one of these three unrelated, pre-existing constraints even if `fk_access_requests_user` itself were missing, misnamed, or missing its CASCADE rule. This is exactly the 'coincidentally-similar but wrong constraint' risk named in the review brief, and it is not a remote edge case here — three real rows in `key_column_usage` already match the loose shape of the query before 004 contributes a fourth.
findings.recommendation: Scope the query explicitly to the object under test on every join key: `SELECT rc.DELETE_RULE FROM information_schema.key_column_usage kcu JOIN information_schema.referential_constraints rc ON rc.CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA = kcu.CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA AND rc.CONSTRAINT_NAME = kcu.CONSTRAINT_NAME WHERE kcu.CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA = DATABASE() AND kcu.TABLE_NAME = 'access_requests' AND kcu.COLUMN_NAME = 'user_id' AND kcu.REFERENCED_TABLE_NAME = 'users' AND kcu.CONSTRAINT_NAME = 'fk_access_requests_user'` and assert `DELETE_RULE = 'CASCADE'` on that single scoped row. Anchoring on the constraint name plus TABLE_NAME plus CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA together rules out both the cross-table collision (user_settings/chats/calculations) and a hypothetical cross-schema collision if the same MariaDB instance ever hosts more than one database with this table name (e.g. a shared CI container running multiple test runs).

findings.description: Per the review brief, the exact query used for the admin-seed assertion wasn't reproducible from available artifacts (no persisted implementer report/script exists in work/access-control/logs — checked; only the task file's own smoke text is authoritative, which specifies `SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE role='admin'` and 'ровно две строки'). That IS a correct cardinality-plus-identity check IF implemented as a strict equality/diff against the full result set (COUNT and content in one assertion). But the brief's mention of 'COLLATE utf8mb4_bin ordering' suggests the implementer added an explicit collation to the query — plausibly to force a deterministic, case-sensitive sort/compare. That detail cuts both ways and needs to be pinned down explicitly rather than assumed: (a) if it's used correctly, it's actually the right defensive move, because MariaDB VARCHAR PK columns commonly default to a case-insensitive collation (e.g. utf8mb4_general_ci/utf8mb4_unicode_ci), under which `id = 'RoGogDBD'` would also match a row inserted as `'rogogdbd'` or `'ROGOGDBD'` — a real risk given the two admin logins are hardcoded verbatim and any case mismatch between the migration's literal and the login Yandex actually returns would go undetected by a case-insensitive `=` comparison; (b) but if the check is 'run a query ORDER BY id COLLATE utf8mb4_bin and eyeball/grep the two expected logins' rather than a hard equality assertion on the full row set, it proves 'these two are present' but not 'no third row is also role=admin' — a LIMIT-bounded or presence-style (grep -q) check would pass identically whether there are exactly 2 admin rows or 5.
findings.recommendation: Require two independent assertions, not one: (1) `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE role='admin'` = 2 exactly (cardinality — this is also the task's own Acceptance Criteria wording, so it should be the literal assertion, not inferred from a row listing); (2) a case-sensitive set-equality check on identity — e.g. `SELECT id FROM users WHERE role='admin' AND BINARY id IN (BINARY 'RoGogDBD', BINARY 'irina2000aleshina')` returning COUNT 2, which simultaneously proves the two rows are exactly the intended logins in the intended case and (combined with assertion 1) that there is no third admin row. Document the exact query in decisions.md so a future round doesn't have to reverse-engineer what 'COLLATE utf8mb4_bin' was protecting against.

findings.description: The idempotency re-verification design is described as 're-apply, confirm admin count stays 2' — that's necessary but not sufficient as a success criterion. It correctly follows the task's explicit instruction to feed the raw file content directly to the mariadb client a second time (bypassing migrate.go's schema_migrations version-skip, which would trivially no-op the second run and prove nothing about the SQL's own idempotency — good that this distinction is respected per tasks/1.md's 'не через docker compose, а напрямую тем же способом'). But 'admin count stays 2' alone is a read-back of state that was already true before the second run started. A second run that fails partway through — e.g., errors on `ADD CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS` due to a MariaDB CLI quirk, or on the INSERT — would leave the admin count unchanged at 2 (because the first run already committed those rows), and a check that only re-reads the count afterward would report a false-positive 'idempotent' result while masking a real second-run failure. The Acceptance Criteria text is explicit that this is a separate requirement: 'повторный прогон того же файла также проходит без ошибок' (the run itself succeeding) is listed alongside, not folded into, the row-count requirement.
findings.recommendation: Point B must assert two things independently: (1) the second mariadb-client invocation itself exits 0 and its stdout/stderr contains no `ERROR` line — capture and grep the client's own output, don't infer success from downstream state; (2) only then re-check `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE role='admin'` = 2 (unchanged) and, for completeness, that `SHOW CREATE TABLE access_requests` and `SHOW INDEX FROM users` didn't spawn a duplicate index or duplicate FK/CHECK constraint under a suffixed name (MariaDB sometimes auto-suffixes a constraint name on conflict rather than erroring, which IF NOT EXISTS is meant to prevent, but is worth confirming with the actual index/constraint count, not just presence, on the second run).

findings.description: The task's own Acceptance Criteria requires: 'Миграция 004_access_control применяется на чистой MariaDB 11.4 и на БД с текущей прод-схемой (001+002+003) без ошибок' — two scenarios joined by 'и' (and), not one. Read against migrate.go (server/migrations/migrate.go:32-54): Run() iterates all *.up.sql files in lexicographic order and skips any version already present in schema_migrations. That means 'clean MariaDB' and 'DB with the current prod schema (001+002+003) already applied' are genuinely different code paths, not two descriptions of the same event: (a) fresh empty volume → 001, 002, 003, 004 all execute in the same Run() call, and at the moment 004's `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN ...` executes, the `users` table has zero rows (nothing before 004 inserts into it) — so the ADD COLUMN...NOT NULL DEFAULT backfill-on-existing-rows behavior is exercised on an empty table, which trivially succeeds and proves nothing about backfill correctness; (b) a persistent volume that already has 001-003 recorded in schema_migrations (the real prod redeploy scenario — this app runs continuously and accumulates real Yandex-authenticated users via EnsureUser/upsertUser well before this migration ships) → only 004 executes, against a `users` table that may already contain real, non-admin rows. A standard `docker compose up -d db app` against a fresh checkout's default volume will almost always exercise only scenario (a). Nothing in the described 17 assertions or the Smoke section explicitly seeds schema_migrations with 001/002/003 plus a dummy pre-existing `users` row and then applies 004 alone — the scenario the Acceptance Criteria explicitly names second and the one that matters most for a migration about to ship against a live database with real users.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit scenario-b run to the check design: start a MariaDB container, apply 0001_init/001/002/003 only (or restore a volume snapshot taken before 004 existed), manually INSERT a throwaway non-admin user row (e.g. `INSERT INTO users (id) VALUES ('smoke-test-existing-user')`), then apply 004_access_control.up.sql alone and assert: (1) it succeeds with no error; (2) the pre-existing row now has `role='user'` (not NULL), `has_access=0` (not NULL) — proving the ADD COLUMN default-backfill behaves correctly against real pre-existing data, which is the actual deployment mechanism this migration ships through, not a side effect of a fresh-volume test happening to also pass 001-003 first.

findings.description: The review brief describes the 17 assertions as covering '...index...' existence, which should include `idx_users_role_has_access`. Worth confirming explicitly that the check asserts the index's column order is `(role, has_access)` as declared, not just that an index with that name exists on the `users` table — a same-named index created with columns reversed (`(has_access, role)`) would pass a name-only existence check but changes the index's usefulness for the leftmost-prefix queries the access-check middleware is expected to run.
findings.recommendation: Use `SHOW INDEX FROM users WHERE Key_name='idx_users_role_has_access' ORDER BY Seq_in_index` and assert the column sequence is exactly `role` (Seq_in_index=1) then `has_access` (Seq_in_index=2), not just that the index name appears in the output.
